key_points: Growth signal is mixed and modest: the latest GDPNow nowcast in the snapshot is about 1.2% annualized, below trend. It conflicts with the Fed's 'solid pace' characterization and staff views of AI capex and productivity strength.

Consumer sentiment is extremely depressed (49.5) but rebounded 4.7 points. The roughly 30% drop in oil over the past month should ease household strain and support real spending ahead, so momentum is stabilizing to improving.
Labor-linked activity indicators are steady: claims at 215k, unemployment at 4.2%, and modest payroll gains. That argues against an imminent growth scare.
For yields, below-trend nowcasts give a slight downward tilt to the 2y and 10y. The curve is essentially neutral on this factor.
For risk assets, steady expansion with low claims and strong capex mildly supports equities and tight credit spreads, and gives a slight downward lean for VIX.
This factor alone carries little information for oil, gold, breakevens or the dollar, so those stay near 0.50.

Inflation still elevated: CPI ~4.2% y/y through May (+0.47% m/m), core PCE ~3.4% y/y (+0.32% m/m); Fed minutes show a majority open to firming if inflation persists, and the 2y at 4.14 vs funds midpoint 3.625 already prices hike risk.

WTI down 30% in a month implies sharply softer headline CPI/PCE prints for June-August (energy and base effects), which should trim hike pricing at the front end more than at the long end -> mild bias to lower 2y, steeper 2s10s.
Core remains sticky (tariffs, services, software, AI input costs), limiting how far disinflation can push yields; hence only modest tilts.
Breakevens already at 5th percentile after the oil drop, so further downside from soft headline prints is limited; slight downward lean only.
Next CPI release falls after the 1-week horizon, so 1w signals are near neutral; disinflation modestly supportive for equities/credit and mildly negative for the dollar via fewer expected hikes.

June payrolls +57k are low but in line with slow labor-force growth; the unemployment rate fell to 4.2% from 4.3%, and initial claims are low at 215k (versus 236k a year ago). The labor market looks stable to slightly firmer, not loosening.

The firm labor data removes the labor-weakness trigger for cuts that FOMC doves cited. With a majority open to firming if inflation persists, this tilts front-end yields modestly higher and the curve flatter.
Much of this is likely already priced in: last week's moves (2y +7bp, 10y +11bp) came after the report, so the signals are kept small.
Low layoffs support tight credit spreads, low VIX and equity earnings. Higher real-rate expectations are mildly negative for gold and mildly positive for the dollar.

Risks to the view: the FOMC sees employment risks tilted to the downside (AI-related hiring caution, job growth concentrated in a few sectors). A weak July or August payroll report could reverse the tilt quickly.
Fed funds at 3.50-3.75% (midpoint ~3.63%) while the 2y sits at 4.14%, near its 1y high: the market already prices meaningful hikes over the next year.

June statement was hawkish in tone ('The Committee will deliver price stability', no easing bias), and April minutes showed a majority open to firming if inflation persists. July 8 minutes of the June meeting are a near-term hawkish headline risk, a slight upward tilt for the 2y over 1w.

The case for hikes rested on the energy shock. WTI is down 30% in a month and 10y breakevens are near 1y lows, which undercuts the inflation-persistence argument. A Fed that holds in July and September rather than hiking would likely take hikes out of the curve, a downward bias for the 2y over 1-3m.

Dovish repricing at the front end implies bull steepening of 2s10s from a 1y-low 0.35, a mildly softer dollar, and mild support for gold and equities. Effects on oil, credit spreads and the VIX are small.
Labor data are soft but stable (payrolls +57k, unemployment 4.2%), so neither cuts nor hikes are imminent. Signals are modest, and September SEP/dots are the key 3m event.

Large structural deficits mean steady heavy coupon supply; the 10y has risen 14bp over 3m while breakevens fell 13bp, consistent with a rising real yield and term premium. The April minutes' 10y decomposition also pointed to higher risk premiums.
The week after July 4 brings the 3y/10y/30y auction cycle, which usually draws a modest supply concession at the long end; this is a slight upward tilt for 10y over 1w.
The early-August quarterly refunding is a risk event. Any guidance toward eventual coupon size increases would add term premium, so the 1m-3m skew is toward a higher 10y and a steeper 2s10s.
The front end is shielded: bill-heavy financing is absorbed by money funds and the Fed's reserve management bill purchases, so supply gives little signal for 2y.
July is seasonally a deficit month, so the TGA tends to drift down from post-June-tax highs, which mildly offsets supply pressure through liquidity. The debt ceiling is not binding.

Second-order effects: a higher term premium is a slight headwind to equities and credit spreads, and fiscal-sustainability concern is mildly supportive of gold and mildly negative for the dollar. All are small.
Financial conditions are loose: NFCI -0.50 is unchanged over the year, and HY OAS at 2.74% sits near the 13th percentile of its 1y range. This mildly supports risk assets via carry and momentum.

Reserves are ample and money markets orderly. The Fed's reserve-management bill purchases keep the balance sheet above year-ago levels. There are no funding-stress signals, and quarter-end and tax dates passed calmly. This slightly anchors the front end and favors mild steepening.

Spreads are already tight and VIX is low (23rd percentile), so upside is asymmetric over 3 months. Further tightening is limited, which pushes spread and VIX odds toward or slightly above 0.50 at longer horizons.
Abundant dollar liquidity and risk-on sentiment lean mildly against the dollar. Gold gets a small tailwind from that, from this factor only.
Minutes flag notable vulnerabilities in hedge-fund Treasury basis leverage and private credit. These are tail risks rather than the base case, which tempers the bullish lean on equities.
Dollar index futures net long at the 97th percentile of the past year (24% of open interest): a crowded long. That is a contrarian bearish tilt for the broad dollar, growing with horizon.

E-mini S&P net positioning is at the 97th percentile (least short in a year). The S&P is at the 95th percentile of its range, the VIX is low at 15.8 and HY spreads are at the 13th percentile. Risk appetite looks stretched, a mild contrarian lean toward equity weakness, higher VIX and wider spreads.
VIX futures shorts are being covered (+8k on the week) and are only at the 64th percentile, so short-vol crowding is moderate rather than extreme. The volatility-up tilt is therefore modest.

Treasury futures shorts (TY at the 55th percentile, TU at the 70th) are mid-range and being trimmed. Short covering is a slight downward pressure on yields, but the signal is weak and gives no curve signal.
Gold is near the bottom of its 1-year range after a 13% 3-month fall, while speculative longs sit mid-range (43rd percentile) and are rising. Sentiment looks washed out, a mild bounce bias.
WTI spec length is mid-range (45th percentile) and being cut after a 30% one-month collapse. Little crowding signal, only a slight rebound lean at longer horizons.
Positioning offers no direct read on breakevens, so those are kept at 0.50.

The 30% one-month drop in oil removes the energy-driven inflation pressure abroad. That lets euro-area, UK and Japanese short rates retreat from their conflict highs, and lower global yields spill modestly into US 10y term premium more than into the 2y.

The dollar is at the 77th percentile of its one-year range with DX speculative longs at the 97th percentile. The cease-fire and risk-on precedent in the minutes weakened the dollar, so the tilt is toward mild dollar softness over 1-3 months.

Energy-importing economies (Europe, Asia, EM) benefit from cheaper oil, and China's growth is described as solid. A better global growth mix plus a softer dollar mildly supports US equities and gold and slightly favours tighter HY spreads and a lower VIX.
Foreign central banks easing relative to a Fed on hold would partly offset dollar weakness. The global channel to breakevens and oil is ambiguous, so those stay near 0.50.
The signals are second-order for US assets, so deviations from 0.50 are kept small.
WTI has collapsed from a 114.58 peak to 69.73 (-30% 1m, -38% 3m) as the Middle East conflict premium unwinds. Price action has stabilized over the past week (-0.8%).

The futures curve was described as steeply backwardated, which implies a modest downward roll drift in spot. Spec length is mid-range (45th percentile), so there is no squeeze signal. Net lean is slightly lower oil, with two-sided geopolitical bounce risk.

Lagged pass-through of the energy drop into headline CPI and PCE prints over the coming months should erode near-term inflation compensation. That points to modest downside for breakevens, despite their already low level (2.23, 5th percentile).

Fading energy inflation lowers the risk of the Fed hikes flagged in the April minutes and revives the scenario of cuts later in the year. That gives slight downside to 2y yields, less to 10y, and a mild bull-steepening tilt to 2s10s.
Cheaper oil is a mild positive for consumers, real incomes and equities, and slightly calming for VIX and HY spreads. At about $70 there is no energy-sector credit stress.

Gold has fallen alongside the inflation-hedge unwind and sits at the 3rd percentile of its 1y range. The commodity disinflation impulse gives only a slight negative lean. The dollar effect is roughly neutral.

The Middle East conflict premium has largely unwound. WTI is down 30% in 1m and back near year-ago levels, gold sits at the 3rd percentile of its 1y range, VIX is at the 23rd percentile and HY spreads at the 13th, so markets price near-full de-escalation.

With calm priced, the remaining geopolitical risk is skewed toward re-escalation or a failure of the cease-fire. That tilts mildly toward higher VIX, oil, gold and HY spreads and slightly lower equities, more so at longer horizons.

The FOMC minutes flag a risk that tariff rates could be increased above present levels. Run-up to the November midterms (beyond the 3m window) could bring trade or fiscal headlines, adding a modest upside tilt to inflation compensation and risk premia.

Rates effects are ambiguous: a risk-off flight to quality pulls yields down, while an energy-driven inflation impulse pushes front-end and breakevens up. Signals for DGS2, DGS10 and 2s10s stay near neutral, with a small dollar safe-haven tilt.
Further de-escalation would remove little additional premium from already-depressed oil, gold and VIX levels, which limits the downside, though the magnitude of tilts is kept small.

thesis: The 30% one-month collapse in oil undercuts the energy-driven case for Fed hikes. Yet the 2y at 4.14% still sits about 50bp above the funds midpoint, pricing hike risk. Softer headline inflation prints over the summer and a Fed that holds in July and September should take some hikes out of the front end. That biases the 2y lower and 2s10s steeper (bull steepening from a 1y-low 0.35), with the 10y held up partly by supply and term premium. A crowded dollar long (DX specs at the 97th percentile), together with risk-on and cheaper energy abroad, tilts the dollar softer over 1-3 months. Equities keep their positive drift, supported by loose financial conditions, solid labor data and lower energy, though stretched positioning tempers the upside. Gold at the 3rd percentile of its range with rising spec length gets a mild rebound bias. Tight HY spreads and low VIX make the 3-month risks two-sided to slightly wider and higher, given geopolitical re-escalation risk. Breakevens lean slightly lower as energy pass-through hits the prints. The pooled log-odds are shrunk substantially because the views are correlated: many strategists lean on the same oil-disinflation story.
